Structural and positional encodings

Source: R/graph-transformers.R
positional-encodings.Rd

Node level encodings that give attention models information about graph structure.

Usage

laplacian_pe(g, k = 8L, use_rspectra = TRUE)

random_walk_pe(g, k = 8L)

shortest_path_distances(g, max_dist = 10L, directed = FALSE)

random_sign_flip(pe, seed = NULL)

add_positional_encoding(g, type = c("random_walk", "laplacian"), k = 8L)

Arguments

g

A graph_data object.

k

Number of encoding dimensions.

use_rspectra

Use RSpectra sparse eigensolvers (if installed) for graphs larger than 500 nodes.

max_dist

Distances above this are clipped to max_dist + 1.

directed

Follow edge direction.

pe

A positional encoding matrix.

seed

Optional integer seed.

type

"laplacian" or "random_walk".

Value

An N by k matrix (laplacian_pe(), random_walk_pe()) or an N by N integer matrix.

Details

  • laplacian_pe(): the k eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized Laplacian \(L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}\) with the smallest nonzero eigenvalues (Dwivedi et al. 2020). Direction is ignored (the adjacency is symmetrized). Eigenvectors are defined only up to sign, and up to a rotation within repeated eigenvalues, so the encoding is not permutation equivariant as a function: a permuted graph can give different signs. Train with random sign flips (random_sign_flip()) to make a model robust to this. Graphs with fewer than k + 1 nodes are padded with zero columns.

  • random_walk_pe(): the return probabilities \([(D^{-1}A)^t]_{ii}\) for \(t = 1, \dots, k\) (Dwivedi et al. 2022). This encoding is permutation equivariant and has no sign ambiguity. It forms dense matrix powers, \(O(k n^3)\) time.

  • shortest_path_distances(): the all pairs hop distance matrix, with unreachable pairs set to max_dist + 1; used as attention bias by graph_transformer_model(). Equivariant: permuting nodes permutes rows and columns.

add_positional_encoding() appends the encoding to the node features of g (or of every graph in a list).

Examples

g <- dataset_karate()
dim(laplacian_pe(g, 4))
#> [1] 34  4
dim(random_walk_pe(g, 3))
#> [1] 34  3
shortest_path_distances(g)[1:3, 1:3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    1    1
#> [2,]    1    0    1
#> [3,]    1    1    0
